The Overcoat. Nikolai Gogol's The Overcoat is a masterpiece of bureaucratic absurdity and human tragedy, following a minor copying clerk whose sole ambition is to acquire a new overcoat. When a thief steals his prized possession, the humble man's desperate plea to authority crumbles into despair, transforming a tale of petty longing into a meditation on dignity, poverty, and the invisible suffering of the overlooked. The protagonist Akaky Akakievich is a lowly copying clerk whose existence is entirely consumed by his work, barely earning enough to sustain himself. He spends years saving to purchase a new overcoat, his singular dream representing the hunger for respectability and a moment of personal pride. After finally acquiring the coat and experiencing a brief social awakening, a group of thieves steals it from him on his way home. Akaky visits an Important Person of rank seeking help, only to be humiliated and dismissed—the system offers no protection for the powerless. The story ends ambiguously with Akaky's death, though rumors circulate of his ghost now stealing overcoats from officials in supernatural revenge. Gogol's narrative voice oscillates between mockery and sympathy, creating an unsettling tension that elevates the tale beyond simple comedy, establishing him as a master of grotesque realism.
